q-sets.input: A search query typed by a user, including repeated words and mixed case.
q-sets.output: One set of distinct normalized words to use when scoring documents.
q-sets.scope: This check concerns query words. It does not retrieve or rank documents.
q-sets.example: How repeated words become one search term

c-latest.input: An iterable of document records from an import, with several versions of the same identity.
c-latest.output: One winning record per tenant and document, sorted by identity.
c-latest.scope: The records are already loaded. Equal versions use the last payload in this warm-up; the later event exercise has a different conflict rule.

c-counts.input: Document records with category labels already assigned.
c-counts.output: A dictionary giving the number of documents for each exact category.
c-counts.scope: You count supplied labels. You do not classify documents or combine spelling variants.
c-counts.example: How documents contribute to category counts

p-fastapi.input: A GET /search request and the supplied in-memory document repository.
p-fastapi.output: A validated HTTP response containing matching document IDs and titles.
p-fastapi.scope: Implement repository lookup and route mapping. This pack uses substring matching and insertion order, not the later ranked-search rules.
p-fastapi.example: From a URL to a search response

p-ingest.input: A batch of document payloads and a store that may already contain earlier copies.
p-ingest.output: Updated stored documents and the batch result required by the contract.
p-ingest.scope: Content is already extracted. This exercise increments a local version when content or source changes; it does not order externally versioned events.
p-ingest.example: What changes when the same batch is retried

q-version.input: A sequence of updates and deletions carrying source versions.
q-version.output: A decision to accept or ignore a delayed event using the newest stored version.
q-version.scope: Reason about source revisions and deletion history. These versions are different from the preceding ingestion lesson's local counter.
q-version.example: Why an old update must not undo a deletion

c-events.input: Source-versioned events and the current in-memory state for each document.
c-events.output: Updated state that retains the newest revision, including a marker after deletion.
c-events.scope: You implement the event rules. Durable delivery and atomic database writes are design extensions.
c-events.example: Follow an update, a deletion and a late retry

q-score.input: Distinct query terms and one document's title and body.
q-score.output: The document's score: 3 points for title membership and 1 for body membership per query term.
q-score.scope: This check calculates relevance only. Access checks and result ordering come later.

g-score.input: The caller's query-term set and one supplied Document.
g-score.output: One integer score for that document.
g-score.scope: Implement score_document only. The shared file's permissions, categories and full search are separate checkpoints.

q-tenants.input: The request's tenant and user, plus one document's sharing information.
q-tenants.output: A yes/no decision about whether this user can read the document.
q-tenants.scope: Assume the request identity is already established. Public means readable within its tenant, not across all tenants.
q-tenants.example: Which users pass both access checks

g-permissions.input: Trusted tenant/user values and a supplied Document with its public flag and allowed users.
g-permissions.output: True or False from the permission helper.
g-permissions.scope: Implement access checking only. Authentication and permission storage are supplied assumptions.
g-permissions.example: Which users pass both access checks

q-filter.input: A document's assigned categories and a requested filter that may be None, empty or populated.
q-filter.output: A decision about whether the document passes the category filter.
q-filter.scope: These three input states have different meanings in this contract. Labels are already assigned.
q-filter.example: Compare an omitted filter with an empty selection

g-categories.input: The document's category set and the caller's optional category filter.
g-categories.output: True or False from the category helper.
g-categories.scope: Implement category matching only. Do not normalize labels or change the meaning of None and an empty set.
g-categories.example: Compare an omitted filter with an empty selection

q-limit.input: Matching documents, their scores, the user's access and a requested page size.
q-limit.output: A full page of readable matches when enough eligible records exist.
q-limit.scope: Choose the order of filtering, ranking and limiting. Index construction is taught after full-scan search.
q-limit.example: Why removing private results after limiting loses a slot

g-search.input: A document iterable, a query, access information, category filter and result limit.
g-search.output: Readable SearchHit records ordered by score and the specified tie-break.
g-search.scope: Combine the helpers in the shared file. This baseline still reads every document for each query.
g-search.example: Follow documents through filtering and ranking

c-search.input: Supplied documents and search options, including tenant, user, categories and limit.
c-search.output: A deterministic, limited list of readable SearchHit records.
c-search.scope: This optional recap repeats full-scan search independently. It does not build a persistent index.
c-search.example: Follow documents through filtering and ranking

c-index-build.input: An open SQLite connection and an iterator of bounded DocumentChunk records from ingestion. Each chunk refers to shared Document metadata; there is no full body field.
c-index-build.output: Document metadata stored once, chunk identities/text and term-to-chunk rows, plus the chunk count.
c-index-build.scope: Tests supply extracted chunks so you can implement storage first. The later chunking exercise implements their producer from streamed words. This task appends unique chunks with consistent metadata; updates and deletion are separate. Older SearchUnit drafts need adapting; export before resetting.
c-index-build.example: Two chunks share one document title and access rule

c-index-query.input: An existing chunk index, a new query, trusted tenant/user IDs and a result limit.
c-index-query.output: Ranked IndexedHit records containing IDs, titles and scores.
c-index-query.scope: Read term_chunks, join shared document metadata, and rank in SQL. Tests seed rows independently. load_chunks fetches only returned text and rechecks document access.
c-index-query.example: How query words find and score stored rows

c-fts.input: A supplied FTS5 database for one customer, a query, user ID and result limit.
c-fts.output: The best readable article matches using SQLite's built-in text ranking.
c-fts.scope: Setup and query preparation are provided. FTS5 maintains its own word index as articles change. This exercise requires all query words and uses default FTS5 rank, unlike the manual index's OR matching and 3/1 weights. The supplied fixtures hold complete short articles; this task covers querying, not large-file ingestion.
c-fts.example: How MATCH finds readable support articles

c-chunking.input: ExtractedDocument records pairing shared Document metadata with one-pass word iterators, plus max_words. The supplied plain-text reader reads bounded blocks and limits word length.
c-chunking.output: DocumentChunk records with at most max_words words and nonempty chunk IDs starting at 0 per document.
c-chunking.scope: Chunking runs before indexing. Tests supply streamed words; demo.py connects file reader, chunker, builder, query and selected-text loading. No full body string is required. PDF/OCR is outside the task.
c-chunking.example: Five streamed words become three identified chunks

q-context.input: Text sections already sorted by relevance and a remaining context budget.
q-context.output: A selection that keeps useful sections in order while staying within the budget.
q-context.scope: Retrieval has already happened. The illustrative token trace explains selection; the quick check and coding contract use whitespace-separated words.
q-context.example: How skipping a large section leaves room for a smaller one

c-context.input: A limited set of ranked text chunks from retrieval, with tenant/document/chunk IDs and caller-scoped access. load_chunks supplies these records in the indexed path.
c-context.output: Bounded context text, matching citation labels and the words used.
c-context.scope: In the indexed pipeline, search_index() ranks IDs and load_chunks() supplies their text. This exercise starts there: it selects whole chunks and labels them, without calling a model. The budget limits selected text; deduplication state still grows with inspected chunk identities.
c-context.example: Which chunks fit, and where their citations point

a-refactor.input: Existing async functions with shared mutable state and unnecessarily slow I/O.
a-refactor.output: The same public behavior with fresh request state and overlapping independent work.
a-refactor.scope: Repair the supplied functions. The fake I/O keeps this exercise local; production capacity limits are a separate concern.
a-refactor.example: What two requests share and what they should own

a-fetch.input: Requested IDs, possibly repeated, and a supplied asynchronous fetch function.
a-fetch.output: One result per original ID position, with repeated IDs sharing a lookup.
a-fetch.scope: You coordinate the supplied calls and cap active work. You do not implement a network client or a cross-request cache.
a-fetch.example: How repeated IDs share a bounded set of lookups

q-cancel.input: A parent request with child tasks still running when the caller cancels.
q-cancel.output: A cancellation response after the parent stops and awaits its owned child work.
q-cancel.scope: Choose the cleanup behavior. Cancellation is not an ordinary failed search result.
q-cancel.example: What happens to child tasks when the caller leaves

a-federated.input: A mapping from source names to supplied search callables. Each callable accepts the query and returns a list of Candidate document IDs and comparable scores within its own access scope.
a-federated.output: Merged ranked hits and the names of sources that failed.
a-federated.scope: Each source owns its retrieval implementation. You schedule calls, enforce the per-source timeout after acquiring a slot, combine results and clean up owned work. The active-call cap does not bound the number of task objects or retained hits.
a-federated.example: Combine successful searches while retaining failures

a-parser.input: An async stream of decoded text fragments; network boundaries may split JSON records.
a-parser.output: Validated StreamEvent records as complete lines become available.
a-parser.scope: Byte decoding happens upstream. You frame and validate text records, preserving the unfinished suffix between reads.
a-parser.example: Reassemble a message split across two reads

a-llm.input: Supplied primary and backup providers yielding fragments of generated text, plus timeout settings. These stream fragments are different from retrieved document chunks.
a-llm.output: One coherent stream of chunks, with fallback only when the contract permits it.
a-llm.scope: The providers are local fakes. You manage stream lifetime and failures, not prompts, retrieval or a real model API.
a-llm.example: Compare failure before and after the first visible chunk

u-upload.input: A seekable binary source and a supplied session that knows the acknowledged upload offset.
u-upload.output: A completed upload whose accepted prefix survives retries.
u-upload.scope: You transfer bounded parts and resume from storage's offset. Text extraction and search happen after upload completion.
u-upload.example: Resume after storage accepts bytes but its reply is lost

u-batch.input: A one-pass stream of unique file IDs and a supplied upload callback.
u-batch.output: Ordered per-file outcomes from a fixed number of worker tasks.
u-batch.scope: The callback owns each file's bytes and resume state. You coordinate the batch; the result metadata still grows with the number of files.
u-batch.example: How workers take the next file when a slot is free

u-extract.input: Bounded byte blocks from a completed UTF-8 text upload.
u-extract.output: Nonempty decoded lines, preserving spaces and carriage returns, that the supplied revision adapter can index.
u-extract.scope: extract_lines() splits on LF (newline) only and skips empty lines. Whitespace-only lines are retained. The supplied adapter commits the lines as one FTS5 revision. PDF/OCR and durable workers are not implemented.
u-extract.example: Decode a character split between byte blocks

s-api.input: A search endpoint whose route mixes request parsing, search decisions and data access.
s-api.output: A proposed division of responsibilities, interfaces and error responses.
s-api.scope: Explain the design and its trade-offs. This activity asks for a written architecture answer, not running service code.
s-api.example: Trace one search across the proposed components

s-ingestion.input: Document changes committed to primary storage while search updates may fail or arrive late.
s-ingestion.output: A design that durably tracks pending indexing and rejects stale destination writes.
s-ingestion.scope: Describe storage, retry and recovery responsibilities. The coding exercises model version rules; they do not supply a durable job system.
s-ingestion.example: Recover a saved document whose indexing job was lost

s-large-import.input: A proposed portal with large tenant imports, source files and search-freshness requirements.
s-large-import.output: An architecture and capacity estimate covering uploads, extraction, indexing and current access.
s-large-import.scope: The volumes and freshness goals are assumptions to validate. Local upload exercises demonstrate bounded transfer and UTF-8 extraction, not production import capacity.
s-large-import.example: Follow a file from upload to searchable text

s-search.input: A growing collection where repeated scans no longer meet the search requirement.
s-search.output: A retrieval design with explicit access, ranking, pagination and freshness choices.
s-search.scope: Explain which measured costs justify an index or search service. The local index exercise is not a large-scale benchmark.
s-search.example: Trace a search without scanning every body

s-latency.input: A request that calls several downstream sources under one response deadline.
s-latency.output: A plan for allocating time, cancelling unfinished work and reporting partial results.
s-latency.scope: Define the caller-visible behavior as well as timeouts. No production network or latency benchmark is supplied.
s-latency.example: What to return when one source misses the deadline

s-chat.input: A user question and documents whose access and versions may change.
s-chat.output: A retrieval-to-answer design with bounded evidence and verifiable source references.
s-chat.scope: Explain how retrieval, context selection and reference checks connect. The course's code constructs context; it does not call or grade a real model.
s-chat.example: Trace an answer reference back to the source text
